Subject: An Interesting Insight on Commonplace Books

Dear Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

I wanted to share a fascinating piece of historical context regarding the "commonplace book," which was highly popular during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. These notebooks were used to gather quotes and excerpts from one's literary wanderings, effectively serving as a personalized encyclopedia of quotations.

In his 1721 essay, "A Letter of Advice to a Young Poet," Jonathan Swift remarked that a commonplace book is something "a provident poet cannot subsist without." He offered this proverbial reason: that great wits have short memories.

The English physician and philosopher John Locke (1632-1704) was all too aware of the grip of amnesia and the shortness of memory. In his seminal work, the *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689), he wrote about his rival Blaise Pascal, whom he named the "prodigy of parts" because he "forgot nothing of what he had done, read, or thought."

In reaction to this, Locke attempted to simulate Pascal's "hyperthymesia" not in the mind, but upon the page. He did this through the construction of a system of "commonplacing," which he viewed as a form of what Swift called "supplemental memory."

I hope this historical detail adds value to your understanding of the topic. Please feel free to reach out if you need any further information.

Warm regards,

We just arrived in Burnham Thorpe, the humble birthplace of Admiral Nelson, after a few hours through winding byways. It's a tiny hamlet where the cottages are mean-looking and straggling with red tiles, lacking the artistic beauty of the average English village—the picturesque thatched roofs and brilliant flower gardens are entirely wanting.

Nelson was the son of the village rector, but the parsonage in which he was born was pulled down many years ago. Still standing and kept in good repair is the church where his father preached. The lectern, as the pulpit-stand in English churches is called, was fashioned of oak taken from Nelson's flagship, the Victory.

The father is buried in the churchyard and a memorial to Nelson has been erected in the church. Meanwhile, the tomb of the admiral rests in St. Paul's Cathedral in London.

Instead, he turned to the wisdom of a friend who, venturing into the wild reedbeds, confirmed that bitterns do boom without any artificial aid. 🔹 In the United States, however, "African" never had such a restricted use except in a very few localities.
🔹 From the North, the practice of using "African" as a descriptive title for free colored people became very extensive and continued up to the middle of the century.

This era saw the existence of African societies, churches, and schools in all the prominent centres of this population. It stands as a powerful testament to the dignity and intellect of our ancestors during a challenging time.

Recent media reports have sparked debate, claiming the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) refused to share information regarding Narendra Modi's education credentials. The PMO's official response was clear: such information is not in their records, and therefore, they cannot provide it.

While this stance is factually correct, it warrants a closer look at the legal framework. Section 2(j) of the RTI Act clearly defines the conditions under which a public authority must provide information. A public authority, like the PMO, is only obliged to share data if it is held by them or under their control. No existing law mandates that the PMO possess details of the educational credentials or degrees of the Prime Minister. Consequently, the PM is under no obligation to submit degree certificates or provide detailed educational history to the PMO upon assuming office.

This logic holds true for other institutions as well. For instance, the Election Commission of India (ECI) does not require contesting candidates to submit academic degree certificates. Candidates are only required to mention their academic credentials in their affidavit; the ECI does not independently enquire into the specifics of these mentioned details.

The key takeaway is that unless the information is in the possession of the requesting authority, a "refusal" to provide it is simply a confirmation that the information does not exist in their files.

While early church fathers largely lacked direct Hebrew knowledge, relying instead on the Alexandrine Greek version (which included apocryphal books), the distinction between canonical and non-canonical texts remained blurred for centuries. In his *Prologus Galeatus*, he explicitly stated that apocryphal books like Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees are read "for the edification of the people, not for authority in establishing church doctrines." This distinction was echoed by Rufinus, though Augustine's stance remained wavering. The controversy deepened until the Council of Hippo (A.D. 393), where apocryphal books were still listed among sacred texts, leaving the canon an open question for centuries. It was not until the Roman Council of Trent that the apocryphal books were firmly included in the Old Testament canon—excluding only Esdras and the Prayer of Manasseh—while those who disagreed were pronounced anathema. In stark contrast, Protestant churches have unanimously adhered to the Hebrew canon, separating the apocryphal books as useful for reading but devoid of authority in matters of faith. Understand the full history, every name, and every number that shaped the Bible you hold today.

But Jerome, who translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew, understood perfectly the distinction between the canonical and the apocryphal books. The canon which he has given agrees with that of the Palestine Jews. He says (Prologus Galeatus) of the apocryphal books Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, that the church reads these "for the edification of the people, not for authority in establishing church doctrines." But the Romish Council of Trent included the apocryphal books in the canon of the Old Testament, with the exception of Esdras and the prayer of Manasseh, pronouncing an anathema on all who should hold a contrary opinion. Dear Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

I wanted to share some reflections on the recent work by Ibsen, specifically regarding the technical feat of carrying through the entire action of a four-act play without a single break. This achievement has been much commented on and admired, particularly because the imaginary time of the drama is often shorter than the real time of representation, as the poet does not even leave intervals for changing scenes.

However, I believe this feat is more curious than important, as nothing particular is gained by such a literal observance of the unity of time. Instead, I feel a definite sense in *John Gabriel Borkman* similar to what we felt vaguely in *Little Eyolf*: that the poet's technical staying-power is beginning to fail him. It seems the initial design was larger and more detailed than the finished work.

If we compare the last acts of *The Wild Duck* and *Hedda Gabler* with the last acts of *Little Eyolf* and *Borkman*, we will see that in the earlier plays, the narrative relaxes towards the close to make room for pure imagination and lyric beauty. The actual drama is often over long before the curtain falls; in the first case, we have Rita and Allmers, and in the other, Ella and Borkman, looking back over their shattered lives and playing chorus to their own tragedy.

For my part, I set the highest value on these choral odes, these mournful antiphones, in which the poet definitely triumphs over the mere playwright. They seem to me noble and beautiful in themselves, and as truly artistic, if not as theatrical, as any abrupter catastrophe could be.

That said, I am not quite sure that they are exactly the conclusions the poet originally projected, and still less am I satisfied that they are reached by precisely the paths which he at first designed to pursue.

He frequently returned to Furlongs, the cottage of Peggy Angus, where some of his most famous works were carried out, such as Tea at Furlongs.

As well as watercolours, Ravilious engraved more than four hundred illustrations and drew over forty lithographic designs for books and publications during his lifetime for large publishing houses such as Jonathan Cape, Lanston Corporation and smaller, less commercial publishers, such as the Golden Cockerel Press, the Curwen Press and the Cresset Press. His woodcut of two Victorian gentlemen playing cricket has appeared on the front cover of every edition of Wisden Cricketers' Almanack since 1938.

In 1940 Ravilious was appointed an official war artist, with the rank of Honorary Captain in the Royal Marines. During that year he painted at the Royal Naval Barracks at Chatham and Sheerness; sailed to Norway and the Arctic on board HMS Highlander, which was carrying out escort duties, and painted submarines at Gosport and coastal defences at Newlyn.

Transform humble calf feet into an exquisite culinary masterpiece with this classic recipe. Start by boiling four perfectly cleaned calf feet (hoofs removed) until tender, then strain the rich broth through a colander. Once cooled, skim the grease and pour the jelly into a skillet, reserving the dregs at the bottom. You should yield approximately two quarts of jelly from these four feet. To this base, add one quart of white wine, the strained juice of six fresh lemons, one and a half pounds of powdered loaf sugar, a touch of pounded cinnamon and mace, and the thinly pared rinds of two lemons.

Carefully wash eight eggs, whip their whites to a froth, crush the shells, and combine everything with the jelly. Set the mixture on the fire, stirring occasionally only until the jelly melts, then let it boil until it becomes perfectly clear on one side while the dross accumulates on the other. Remove the thickest layer of impurities with care, pour the liquid through a bag made of cotton or linen suspended in a purpose-built frame, and replace the filtrate until the jelly is completely transparent. Cover with a lid to keep out dust, then serve in glasses where the jelly looks its most beautiful when broken.

Pro Tip: For the palest jelly, use hog feet; for a stunning, beautiful amber hue, choose sheep feet.

There should be from four feet, about two quarts of jelly: pour into it one quart of white wine, the juice of six fresh lemons strained from the seeds, one pound and a half of powdered loaf sugar, a little pounded cinnamon and mace, and the rind thinly pared from two of the lemons; wash eight eggs very clean, whip up the whites to a froth, crush the shells and put with them, mix it with the jelly, set it on the fire, stir it occasionally till the jelly is melted, but do not touch it afterwards. The bag should be made of cotton or linen, and be suspended in a frame made for the purpose. The feet of hogs make the palest coloured jelly; those of sheep are a beautiful amber-colour, when prepared.

The strategic importance of Cricklade as a station on the upper Thames goes far beyond its role as a crossing point for a major road; it marks the critical junction where the Churn, the first important tributary stream, joins the Thames. 

Above this confluence, the Thames is barely a stream. Even in the eighteenth century and earlier, prior to the digging of the Severn and Thames Canal, its volume depended entirely on the weather, meaning that mills at Somerford Keynes were likely not continuously worked throughout the year, regardless of whether modern engineering was later applied to maintain the supply. 

However, once the Churn—known to have a larger volume of water than the Thames itself—falls into Cricklade, the two waters combine to form a true river. Understanding the Financial Scope of Ombudsman Awards: Key Limits You Need to Know

When it comes to compensation awards directed by the Ombudsman, here are the critical financial boundaries:

• **Compensation Cap:** The amount awarded cannot exceed the actual loss suffered by the complainant or **Rs 20 lakh**, whichever is lower.
• **Exclusive Basis:** Compensation is calculated exclusively on the amount involved in the dispute itself.
• **Additional Compensation:** The Ombudsman can also award an additional sum of **Rs 1 lakh** specifically to account for:
  - Loss of the complainant's time
  - Expenses incurred by the complainant
  - Harassment
  - Mental agony suffered by the complainant

Knowing these precise figures ensures transparency and fairness in every resolution.

Regardless of how faulty his specific conclusions may be, Wesley arrived at a pivotal historical viewpoint. This perspective made it impossible to view classical standards—or even the standards of French critics—as holding the "holy sanction of Nature herself."

Subject: A Fun Historical Look at Cat Photography

Dear Customer,

Before LOLCat, Grumpy Cat, Longcat, and Nyan Cat, and long before the modern computer was but a glint in Mother Turing's eye, there were the felines featured in *Kittens and Cats: A First Reader* (1911). This delightful, yet also slightly creepy, book suggests that taking photos of cats and brandishing them with amusing captions was far from a phenomenon born with the internet. Within its pages, we meet "Queen Cat," "Dunce Cat," "Party Cat," and perhaps our favorite "Hero Cat," amongst others.

The book is attributed to the American children's author Eulalie Osgood Grover, who weaves a tale of the Queen's party and all the kitty characters attending. As for the photographs themselves, the book states them to be courtesy of the Rotograph Company, a popular postcard manufacturer, which implies they are almost certainly an early example of the work of Harry Whittier Frees, their staff animal photographer.

A few years later, Frees became associated with a whole host of similar pictures under his own name. This included the 1915 publication of *The Little Folks of Animal Land*, followed by a number of further such collections until he ended his own life in 1953.

How did Frees get his cats to pose for such photographs, even more remarkable before the days of super quick shutter speeds? Although he denied the use of dead or taxidermied animals and insisted only humane methods were used, one can't help but wonder if this is really true, especially in the case of his later work which involved more elaborate tableaus than displayed in this book.

I hope you enjoy this little historical detour into the world of early cat photography!

Best regards,

Subject: Update on Our Research into Early Christian Teachings on Usury

Dear Valued Customer,

I am writing to share some key findings from our recent review of early Christian history regarding the teaching on usury. As you know, the results up to the middle of the fourth century remain inconclusive, a summary well provided by Dr. Cleary:

"Hitherto we have encountered mere prohibitions of usury with little or no attempt to assign a reason for them other than that of positive legislation. Most of the statements of these early patristic writers, as well as possibly all of the early Christian legislative enactments, deal solely with the practice of usury by the clergy; still, there is sufficient evidence to show that in those days it was reprobated even for the Christian laity, for the _Didache_ and Tertullian clearly teach or presuppose its prohibition, while the oecumenical Council of Nice certainly presupposed its illegality for the laity, though it failed to sustain its doctrinal presuppositions with corresponding ecclesiastical penalties. With the exception of some very vague statements by Cyprian and Clement of Alexandria, we find no attempt to state the nature of the resulting obligation--that is to say, we are not told whether there is an obligation of obedience, of justice, or of charity. The prohibition indeed seems to be regarded as universal; and it may very well be contended that for the cases the Fathers consider it was in fact universal--for the loans with which they are concerned, being necessitous, should be, in accordance with Christian charity, gratuitous--even if speculatively usurious loans in general were not unjust.'[1]"

Subject: Understanding the History of Parisian Burial Practices

Dear Valued Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

I am writing to share some fascinating historical context regarding the development of burial infrastructure in Paris during the 1860s. By this time, the catacombs had already become an established solution for the centuries of deceased who had been buried in urban churchyards and burial grounds. Like many major cities, Paris had recently reached a crisis where its former methods of interring the deceased were no longer sustainable.

Eighteenth-century Parisian burial grounds were unfortunately unpleasant places. One of the oldest and largest was the Cimetière des Innocents, where Parisians had been interred since the twelfth century. This cemetery bordered the busy central market of Les Halles. Although attempts had been made to keep the living and the dead separate—such as a wall constructed under King Philippe II Auguste—the market activity still regularly spilled onto the graves, where the odors of decomposing corpses mingled with the detritus of hawkers.

Given that disease was frequently attributed to miasmas, or bad air, there was significant concern that this noxious mix could be dangerous or even fatal. This was tragically highlighted by a ghastly 1780 incident in which the ground in a neighboring cellar broke open, throwing corpses into the basement of a house. Medical expert Antoine-Alexandre Cadet de Vaux gave a report to the Royal Academy of Sciences deploring the "cadaverous exhalations." Ultimately, the cemetery was finally closed, but the question of what to do with the dead remained an open issue until the creation of the catacombs.

Thank you for allowing me to share this intriguing piece of history with you.

Best regards,

🎵 **Auld Lang Syne: More Than Just a New Year's Tradition** 🎵

This year, **Frank C. Stanley** took the stage to perform a timeless classic: **"Auld Lang Syne"**, the poem by the Scotsman **Robert Burns** that traditionally greets us at the stroke of midnight.

But what does the title really mean?
📜 The Scots title translates literally to "old long since," but idiomatically, it evokes "long long ago," "days gone by," or simply "old times." Consequently, the first line of the chorus, "For auld lang syne," can be loosely translated as "for (the sake of) old times."

🔍 **The Truth Behind the Lyrics**
Did Burns write every word himself? Not entirely. He sent a copy of his song to the **Scots Musical Museum** with a humble remark: *"The following song, an old song, of the olden times, and which has never been in print, nor even in manuscript until I took it down from an old man."*

Some lyrics were indeed "collected" rather than composed. The ballad **"Old Long Syne"**, printed in **1711** by **James Watson**, shows considerable similarity in the first verse and chorus to Burns' later poem and is almost certainly derived from the same "old song." While Burns attributed the whole to himself, it is a fair supposition to attribute the rest of the poem to Burns himself, given the unique voice he brought to these collected verses.

Let's raise our glasses to the past and the future together! 🥂

Subject: An Update on Robert John Thornton's "The Temple of Flora"

Dear Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

I am writing to share some fascinating details regarding Robert John Thornton's *The Temple of Flora*, which stands as the third and final part of his illustrated series on the sexual system of Carolus von Linnaeus. This work is widely considered the greatest of all flower books.

The series features sumptuous depictions of flowers set in epic and unusual scenes. Interspersed among these images are various descriptions, histories, and poetic odes about the featured blooms. The first plates were engraved by Thomas Medland in May 1798, based on paintings by Philip Reinagle. Between 1798 and 1807, the project produced a total of thirty-three coloured plates, engraved in aquatint, stipple, and line. Other engravers involved included Joseph Constantine Stadler, who worked from paintings by Peter Charles Henderson.

When Thornton planned the project, he had decided to publish seventy folio-size plates. Unfortunately, a lack of interest from the general public led to financial difficulties; a holding lottery could not save the scheme, nor could a dedicated page honoring Queen Charlotte (the spouse of George III and patroness of botany and the fine arts).
